Lincang.relevance: Lincang sets the upstream cost floor for Chinese primary germanium production. The 850 ppm grade is roughly six times higher than Wulantuga and an order of magnitude higher than typical zinc-byproduct deposits, which means Lincang Xinyuan can extract germanium at lower cost per tonne than any other operator in the world. Anyone producing germanium outside China — Umicore, 5N Plus, the planned Big Hill and Apex projects — has to contend with Lincang's structural grade advantage when competing on price. The deposit's existence is part of why Chinese domestic germanium trades at one-third western pricing.
Lincang.chain_specific_risk: State-affiliated operator under export licensing regime; zero direct western access.

Wulantuga.relevance: Wulantuga is the largest germanium deposit in the world by contained reserves but punches well below its weight in actual output. The 137 ppm average grade and the technical challenges of recovering germanium from low-grade lignite ash mean only an estimated 15-25% of the deposit's theoretical germanium content is commercially extracted. The remainder sits as theoretical headroom that could in principle expand Chinese supply if better extraction technology or higher prices justified the additional capital — but at current operating economics, that headroom is not being realized.
Wulantuga.chain_specific_risk: State ownership means output is policy-driven rather than price-responsive.

Yimin.relevance: Yimin represents the long tail of Chinese coal-hosted germanium resources beyond the named majors. Total resource size is large at around 4,000 tonnes, but the deposits are dispersed across multiple smaller operators with low recovery rates and fragmented disclosure. The basin's contribution to actual refined output is small — perhaps 5-10 t/yr feeding into the Smaller Chinese Refiners aggregate — but it matters for understanding why Chinese germanium supply estimates carry meaningful uncertainty bands. The unrealized resource potential here is part of what makes long-run Chinese supply forecasting difficult.
Yimin.chain_specific_risk: Fragmented operator base, opaque production data.

Huize.relevance: Huize is the upstream resource that anchors the largest single primary germanium output stream in the world. The zinc-byproduct extraction pathway is technically simpler and more economically efficient than coal-ash extraction, which is part of why Chihong's Huize-to-smelter pipeline outperforms Wulantuga on actual output despite Wulantuga having larger contained reserves. Output economics are tied to the underlying zinc-lead operation rather than germanium prices alone — when zinc prices weaken, smelter throughput slows and germanium output falls correspondingly.
Huize.chain_specific_risk: Output tied to zinc pricing, not germanium demand signals.

Yiliang + SYGT.relevance: Yiliang and SYGT serve as supplemental concentrate feedstock to Yunnan Chihong's Qujing smelter, complementing the primary Huize stream. Combined germanium reserves of 186 tonnes are modest compared to Huize's 443 tonnes, but the deposits matter because they extend the operational life of Chihong's vertically integrated zinc-to-germanium pipeline beyond what Huize alone could sustain. Without these supplemental sources, Chihong's primary germanium output would taper as Huize matures.
Yiliang + SYGT.chain_specific_risk: Limited public disclosure on reserves and production.

Spetsugli.relevance: Spetsugli holds reserves of around 1,015 tonnes of contained germanium — meaningful in absolute terms, comparable to Lincang in size. Under different geopolitics this would represent a structurally important supply diversification away from China. Under current sanctions, the entire output flows to Chinese buyers, which paradoxically reinforces rather than challenges Chinese dominance over western germanium markets. The deposit's existence is a reminder that geological supply and market-accessible supply are different things.
Spetsugli.chain_specific_risk: Sanctions-exposed; no western route to market.

Big Hill.relevance: Big Hill is the single most important new western germanium feedstock development of the past decade. Around 700 tonnes of contained germanium sit in tailings that already exist above ground — meaning STL/Gécamines avoids the typical greenfield mining timeline of exploration, permitting, and capital construction. Under offtake to Umicore, the recovered material flows directly to the western chokepoint refinery in Olen, Belgium. If Big Hill ramps successfully, it materially extends the runway of western germanium supply through the late 2020s.
Big Hill.chain_specific_risk: DRC operating risk; reprocessing ramp-up delays possible.

Red Dog.relevance: Red Dog is North America's only commercial germanium-bearing zinc deposit. The germanium content is incidental to the primary zinc-lead operation, but the byproduct stream feeding Teck's Trail smelter has been the only commercial source of North American germanium feedstock for decades. The mine is currently scheduled to deplete by 2031 unless Teck advances the adjacent Aktigiruq extension — which would extend the deposit's operational life but requires its own permitting and capital decision. If neither Aktigiruq nor a similar extension proceeds, North America loses its primary germanium feedstock entirely with Red Dog's closure.
Red Dog.chain_specific_risk: Declining toward planned end-of-mine in 2031 (Aktigiruq extension possible but not yet permitted).

Lincang Xinyuan.relevance: Lincang Xinyuan is the only publicly listed pure-play germanium producer in China and one of the few globally. It mines the world's highest-grade germanium-bearing coal at Lincang and refines the output in-house, capturing margin across the full value chain from raw extraction through finished germanium products. The integrated structure means a single corporate entity controls roughly 40 t/yr of refined Chinese germanium output, all subject to MOFCOM export licensing. The Shenzhen A-share listing gives Chinese investors direct equity exposure to Chinese germanium policy decisions, but the share class is not freely accessible to most western investors.
Lincang Xinyuan.chain_specific_risk: Chinese export controls limit westward flow of output.

Shengli Coal Group.relevance: Shengli Coal Group operates the largest known germanium-bearing coal deposit in the world at Wulantuga in Inner Mongolia. Crude germanium is recovered from coal fly ash and combustion residues during routine power-plant coal use, then sold into the network of smaller Chinese refiners that handle the downstream purification. Output is harder to track than Yunnan-based operators because germanium is incidental to Shengli's primary business of supplying coal to power generators, and individual smelter-level production data is not publicly disclosed.
Shengli Coal Group.chain_specific_risk: Opaque production data and no western investment vehicle.

Yunnan Chihong.relevance: Yunnan Chihong is the largest single primary germanium producer in the world. Crude germanium is recovered from the Huize and Yiliang zinc-lead concentrates as a byproduct of zinc smelting, then refined in-house to germanium dioxide, zone-melted ingots, and fiber-grade germanium tetrachloride that supplies Chinese fiber preform manufacturers including YOFC, Hengtong, and ZTT. All output flows into the Chinese primary supply pool and is subject to MOFCOM export licensing. If Chihong's smelter went offline, roughly 30% of global primary germanium supply would disappear in a single shock.
Yunnan Chihong.chain_specific_risk: Chinese export controls limit direct western access to the output.

JSC Germanium.relevance: JSC Germanium represents the third-country production tier on the germanium chain — neither western nor Chinese, but Russian state-owned and currently sanctioned from western markets. Roughly 20 t/yr of refined germanium that previously flowed to global IR optics and fiber buyers now goes to Chinese and other non-western customers, effectively transferring Russian germanium output into the Chinese supply pool. The node appears on the chain to track the flow rather than because it is investable. If sanctions ever reverse, JSC Germanium would re-enter as a meaningful western-accessible supplemental supplier.
JSC Germanium.chain_specific_risk: Sanctions-exposed; no western route to market.

STL / Gécamines.relevance: STL/Gécamines is the most important new western germanium feedstock supply development of the past decade. Umicore holds the offtake rights on the germanium recovered from Big Hill, which means the project directly supplies the western chokepoint refinery in Olen, Belgium. The first germanium concentrate is expected by 2027 with a target of ~30 t/yr at full ramp. If STL ramps successfully, it materially expands the volume Umicore can refine and reduces western dependency on Chinese primary supply.
STL / Gécamines.chain_specific_risk: DRC operating risk; JV structure and political sensitivity around Gécamines.

Teck Resources.relevance: Teck is North America's only commercial source of germanium-bearing zinc concentrate. The Red Dog mine in northwestern Alaska produces zinc concentrate that is shipped to the Trail smelter in British Columbia, where germanium is recovered as a byproduct of zinc refining. Specific germanium output volumes are not disclosed separately in Teck's filings, but the recovered material flows downstream to Umicore and 5N Plus as feedstock. Red Dog is currently scheduled to deplete by 2031, with the adjacent Aktigiruq extension under evaluation as a potential successor. If Aktigiruq does not advance, North American primary germanium feedstock disappears with Red Dog's closure.
Teck Resources.chain_specific_risk: Red Dog declines toward 2031 end-of-mine; Ge output volumes not separately disclosed.

Lincang Xinyuan Refinery.relevance: The refining capacity that converts Lincang's high-grade coal-extracted germanium into finished products. Together with Yunnan Chihong Refinery and the Smaller Chinese Refiners aggregate, it forms the bulk of the China Primary Supply pool — the 120 t/yr of refined germanium that represents 83% of global primary supply and is subject to MOFCOM export licensing. Investment exposure flows through the parent company's SZSE listing rather than the refinery as a separate entity.
Lincang Xinyuan Refinery.chain_specific_risk: Chinese export licensing controls downstream access.

Yunnan Chihong Refinery.relevance: The refining capacity that converts the largest single primary germanium feedstock stream in the world — the byproduct germanium recovered at the Huize zinc smelter — into fiber-grade GeCl₄ supplying YOFC, Hengtong, ZTT, and other Chinese fiber preform manufacturers. The integrated zinc-to-germanium-to-GeCl₄ pathway gives Chihong Refinery a structural cost advantage over standalone refiners and explains why China's fiber preform industry runs primarily on domestic GeCl₄. Output flows into the Chinese Primary Supply pool. Investment exposure runs through the parent SHSE listing.
Yunnan Chihong Refinery.chain_specific_risk: Output primarily stays within Chinese domestic ecosystem.

JSC Germanium Refinery.relevance: The integrated Russian refining capacity that processes Spetsugli coal-extracted germanium into finished products. Output volumes are similar to PPM Pure Metals — meaningful at around 20 t/yr — but unlike PPM, this capacity is unavailable to western buyers under post-2022 sanctions. The refinery node appears on the chain to track the supply that has shifted from western to Chinese markets, not because it is investable. Russian sanctions are the structural reason the world's third-largest germanium producer no longer participates in western fiber, IR optics, or satellite solar supply chains.

Umicore.relevance: Umicore's Olen facility is the only commercial-scale germanium tetrachloride producer outside China and Russia, which makes it the structural chokepoint for western fiber optic cable manufacturing. It pulls feedstock from two sources: copper-cobalt tailings reprocessed by STL/Gécamines in the DRC, where Umicore holds the germanium offtake rights, and recycled scrap returning from Prysmian and other fiber preform makers. The refined GeCl₄ ships out to every major non-Chinese fiber preform line in the world. If Umicore stopped operating, western fiber manufacturing would lose its primary GeCl₄ supply within months.
Umicore.chain_specific_risk: Single-facility risk at Olen; business distractions from other Umicore segments (batteries, automotive catalysts) create quarterly earnings volatility unrelated to germanium.

5N Plus.relevance: 5N Plus is the second western high-purity germanium refiner alongside Umicore, but with a different operational profile — its output flows primarily into satellite solar cells via AZUR Space rather than fiber-grade GeCl₄. Refining capacity sits in Montreal and Salt Lake City, with the Utah facility scaling up under an $18.1 million US Department of Energy grant awarded January 2026 specifically for germanium recycling. Feedstock comes from Teck Resources zinc concentrate streams plus end-of-life recovered material. 5N Plus is pre-commercial on fiber-grade GeCl₄ but pursuing qualification, which would materially diversify the western refining base if achieved.
5N Plus.chain_specific_risk: Pre-commercial on fiber-grade GeCl₄; qualification timeline and customer adoption unclear.

PPM Pure Metals.relevance: PPM Pure Metals is Europe's second germanium refiner alongside Umicore, operating at smaller scale and focused on zone-refined germanium for IR optics and SiGe semiconductor customers rather than fiber-grade GeCl₄. Estimated output is around 10-15 t/yr — meaningful for European supply diversification but not at the volumes that would replace Umicore in any feedstock disruption scenario. PPM does not feature in the western chokepoint discussion the way Umicore does, but its existence ensures Europe has more than one specialty germanium refiner serving the regional industrial base.
PPM Pure Metals.chain_specific_risk: Private — not directly investable. Scale limited.

China Primary Supply.relevance: China Primary Supply is the single most important node on the germanium chain. It captures the structural reality that 83% of global primary germanium production happens in China, that essentially all of it flows through MOFCOM-licensed export decisions, and that Chinese domestic pricing trades at roughly one-third of western retail levels because of that policy lever. The bifurcated price structure — $2,500/kg in China versus $8,500/kg in the West — exists because of this aggregate's position in the chain. If MOFCOM tightened licensing further, western germanium prices would spike again as they did in late 2024.
China Primary Supply.chain_specific_risk: Export licensing can be tightened or released unilaterally.

Western Recycled Supply.relevance: This aggregate is the entirety of germanium that western fiber preform makers, IR optics manufacturers, defense contractors, and satellite solar producers can rely on without depending on Chinese export licensing or sanctioned Russian supply. It is meaningfully smaller than China Primary Supply — roughly 90-110 t/yr versus 120 t/yr — and it is structurally constrained by the recycled feedstock pool. Adding new western primary supply (Big Hill, Apex) is the only way this aggregate grows materially. The bifurcated pricing structure exists because western buyers compete for limited supply at this layer.
Western Recycled Supply.chain_specific_risk: Feedstock-limited; cannot scale independently of recycled pool or DRC tailings depletion.

Various State Operators.relevance: Various State Operators captures the long tail of smaller Chinese germanium feedstock producers that flow into the Smaller Chinese Refiners aggregate. The category exists because Chinese germanium production is highly fragmented at the source — beyond Yunnan Chihong and Lincang Xinyuan, dozens of smaller state coal operators contribute crude germanium that is harder to attribute to specific named entities. Output stays within the Chinese ecosystem and is subject to the same MOFCOM export licensing as the named majors. Useful for understanding why total Chinese supply estimates carry uncertainty bands.

Chinese State Refiners.relevance: The fragmented portion of Chinese refining capacity that operates outside the named major operators. Important for accurately estimating Chinese supply totals — without this aggregate, China Primary Supply would be undercounted — but each individual constituent is too small to track separately. Output flows into the Chinese Primary Supply pool with the same MOFCOM export licensing exposure as the named majors. The category is a useful reminder that Chinese germanium production is structurally more dispersed than headline market-share figures suggest.
Chinese State Refiners.chain_specific_risk: Opaque individual facility data; output subject to Chinese export controls.

Global Supply.relevance: Global Supply provides the framing for the total germanium market: 230 t/yr is small by industrial commodity standards, comparable to the annual output of a single large copper mine. The chain's smallness is what makes single-facility risks at Olen, Krasnoyarsk, or Qujing structurally meaningful — there is no global market that smooths out localized disruptions because total volume is too thin. Demand sits around 230 t/yr today and is projected to outgrow supply by 2027 as fiber, satellite solar, and IR optics applications expand, which is why new western primary supply is being underwritten across multiple jurisdictions simultaneously.

Blue Moon Metals.relevance: Blue Moon's Apex restart project is the only meaningful primary germanium development in the United States. The mine produced germanium and gallium historically before going on care-and-maintenance under previous owners; Blue Moon is targeting 5-10 t/yr of germanium output starting 2028, contingent on permitting and ramp-up financing. Apex would be the first new western primary germanium source to come online since the Russian sanctions, materially reducing US dependence on Chinese primary supply. The project carries typical junior-mining execution risk — pre-production timing, permitting, and financing — but the strategic positioning has attracted high-quality institutional backing.
Blue Moon Metals.chain_specific_risk: Pre-production junior; permitting, financing, and ramp-up risk typical of early-stage mining projects.

LightPath Technologies.relevance: LightPath sits adjacent to the germanium chain rather than within it. BlackDiamond chalcogenide glass replaces germanium in IR optics applications, so LightPath captures displaced demand whenever germanium prices stay elevated or supply tightens further. The F-35 fighter jet program has validated BlackDiamond as a qualified IR optics material, which opens the path to broader defense and commercial adoption. LightPath does not consume germanium feedstock and does not supply the chain; it appears on the germanium tree as a substitution play. The cleaner the BlackDiamond design-in path becomes, the more germanium demand it will absorb.
LightPath Technologies.chain_specific_risk: Substitution penetration is slow; BlackDiamond requires design-in cycles that take years per customer platform.

Germanium Metal.relevance: Direct physical germanium accumulation is the only way to express a clean view on germanium prices without taking equity-specific operational risk in a refiner or miner. The OTC market structure means buyers must navigate bilateral relationships with producers (Umicore, 5N Plus, PPM, Lincang Xinyuan) or specialty metal traders, and storage and handling logistics matter. Hartree Partners, the commodity stockpile operator backing Blue Moon's Apex restart, is one of the few institutional buyers known to hold physical germanium positions. Most institutional germanium exposure flows through equity rather than physical, but the option exists.
Germanium Metal.chain_specific_risk: Illiquidity amplifies price moves in both directions; no exchange pricing transparency; storage and handling requirements non-trivial.

specialty_metals.name: Specialty Metals
specialty_metals.description: Small-volume metals for chips, fiber, and turbines; mostly refined in China.
specialty_metals.long_description:
Small-volume industrial metals scattered across the AI infrastructure chain — each one used in a very specific application that nothing else can do. Germanium dopes the glass inside fiber optic cables. Gallium goes into the power chips and laser chips that move electrons and light around inside datacenters. Indium makes the lasers in high-speed transceivers. Tantalum sits inside capacitors on every server board. Tungsten and rhenium go into the highest-temperature parts of chip interconnects and gas turbine blades. What unites them is they're almost all produced as byproducts of mining bigger, more common metals, which means you can't just scale up their supply on demand.

Germanium and gallium are the most acute pressure points right now — both are about 80–98% Chinese supplied and both feed AI infrastructure directly. Rhenium is the smallest of the group at around 50 tonnes globally per year and gates how fast gas turbines for onsite datacenter power can be built.

rare_earths.name: Rare Earths
rare_earths.description: Magnet-making elements found in hard drives, fans, and wind turbines; China-refined.
rare_earths.long_description:
Despite the name, these seventeen metals aren't actually rare in the ground — they're just almost never concentrated enough in one place to mine economically, and they're chemically very hard to separate from each other. What makes them important is that a few of them make the strongest magnets ever invented. Those magnets end up inside hard drives, server fans, wind turbines, and the precision machinery that builds AI chips. China refines about 85% of the world's supply.

The most watched ones are dysprosium and terbium, which let those magnets keep working at high temperatures and are almost entirely refined in southern China. Neodymium and praseodymium are the bulk magnet inputs and demand keeps rising as more motors get built into everything from datacenters to EVs.

base_metals.name: Base & Industrial Metals
base_metals.description: High-volume metals like copper and aluminum that show up almost everywhere in the build.
base_metals.long_description:
The metals you'd recognize from any industrial product — copper, aluminum, steel ingredients, lithium. They show up almost everywhere in a datacenter: copper carries every electrical signal and every kilowatt of power, aluminum makes heat sinks and rack frames, nickel goes into stainless steel cooling systems, and lithium goes into the batteries backing up the whole facility. Unlike the specialty metals, these are produced at massive scale and traded on open commodity markets — but datacenters use enough of them that demand from AI buildouts is now noticeable in global pricing.

Copper is the most systemic — a single hyperscale campus consumes thousands of tonnes across its wiring, transformers, and motors, and analysts increasingly see datacenter demand as one of the structural forces driving copper prices over the next decade. Nickel and lithium matter most for the battery side of the chain.

precious_metals.name: Precious Metals
precious_metals.description: Small amounts of gold, silver, and platinum used in contacts, solder, and catalysts.
precious_metals.long_description:
Tiny amounts of gold, silver, and platinum-group metals used where their unique properties matter more than their cost. Gold makes the ultra-fine bond wires that connect chip dies to their packages, and plates the contact pads on circuit boards because it doesn't tarnish. Silver goes into the paste that conducts electricity on the front of every solar panel. Platinum, palladium, and rhodium are catalysts inside fuel cells and emissions control systems. None of these metals are used in large volumes per device, but they're irreplaceable for the specific job each one does.

Silver is the most demand-sensitive — solar panel production consumes 10–15% of global mined silver and that share keeps growing as renewable buildouts accelerate. Platinum-group metals are tracked closely by the fuel cell and emissions control markets.

specialty_gases.name: Specialty Gases
specialty_gases.description: Noble gases used in semiconductor fabs and to seal high-capacity hard drives.
specialty_gases.long_description:
The noble gases that semiconductor factories and high-end hard drives can't operate without. Helium cools the cryogenic equipment inside chip factories and seals high-capacity hard drives so the platters can spin faster without air resistance. Neon, krypton, and xenon are the working gases inside the lasers that pattern the circuits onto silicon wafers — without them, no advanced chip gets made. Argon is the bulk inert gas used across nearly every fab process. These gases are typically separated from air or extracted as byproducts of steel and gas production, so their supply depends on completely unrelated industries.

The most acute risk is xenon, which feeds the lasers in the most advanced lithography machines used for the newest AI chips. Neon supply was disrupted by the Ukraine war (most global neon was a byproduct of Ukrainian steel mills) and has been a watched item ever since.

industrial_chemicals.name: Industrial Gases & Chemicals
industrial_chemicals.description: Bulk reactive chemistries feeding battery, fab, and refrigerant production.
industrial_chemicals.long_description:
The reactive chemistries that show up upstream of almost everything else. Ammonia feeds the nitrogen used in semiconductor manufacturing. Chlorine is needed to turn raw silicon and germanium into the purified forms used in chips and fiber optics. Fluorspar (calcium fluoride) is the entry point for an entire family of fluorine chemicals that end up in refrigerants, fire suppression agents, and the insulating gases inside high-voltage equipment. Sulfuric acid is the workhorse acid used in countless processing steps. None of these chemicals is finished product — they're the reagents that make finished products possible.

Fluorspar is the most strategically watched of the group, since China controls about 65% of global supply and the downstream fluorine chemistry feeds critical applications across multiple industries.

nuclear_materials.name: Nuclear Materials
nuclear_materials.description: Uranium fuel and the zirconium tubing that holds it, for reactors powering datacenters.
nuclear_materials.long_description:
The fuel and structural materials for nuclear reactors. Uranium ore is enriched into two grades: regular low-enriched uranium (LEU) for conventional reactors like the ones supplying Three Mile Island's restart, and high-assay low-enriched uranium (HALEU) for the new small modular reactors being designed for direct datacenter power supply. Zirconium is the metal tubing that physically holds the uranium fuel pellets inside the reactor. As hyperscalers sign nuclear power deals — Microsoft with Three Mile Island, Amazon with X-energy — these materials become directly relevant to AI infrastructure.

HALEU is the most constrained piece by far — currently only Russia and China produce it at commercial scale, with Centrus Energy operating the only US facility at pilot scale. Without HALEU, most SMR designs can't actually fuel up.

battery_materials.name: Battery Materials
battery_materials.description: Cathode and anode inputs for the lithium cells in UPS backup and grid storage.
battery_materials.long_description:
The raw inputs that go into lithium battery cells. Lithium itself is mined from brine pools or hard rock deposits. Iron phosphate forms the cathode (the energy-storing side) of the LFP batteries used in datacenter backup. Graphite forms the anode (the energy-releasing side). Phosphoric acid is needed to make the cathode material. These same inputs feed the batteries powering electric vehicles, grid-scale storage projects, and the UPS systems backing up datacenters — they're all competing for the same supply.

Graphite is one of the more concentrated chokepoints in the chain, with about 70% of global processing in China. Lithium itself is more diversified, with major producers in Australia, Chile, and China.

solar_materials.name: Solar & Storage Specialty
solar_materials.description: Thin-film semiconductors and redox-active metals for solar panels and flow batteries.
solar_materials.long_description:
A small group of materials with specific roles in renewable energy and long-duration storage. Tellurium and cadmium are the active layer in CdTe thin-film solar panels — a different technology from the more common silicon panels, made almost entirely by First Solar. Vanadium has two completely separate uses worth tracking together: it's a catalyst in the emissions control systems on gas turbines, and it's the active electrolyte in vanadium redox flow batteries, an emerging long-duration storage technology that pairs well with renewables.

Vanadium is the most interesting of the group because the same metal feeds two very different theses — gas power emissions control today and grid-scale long-duration storage tomorrow.

petrochemicals.name: Petrochemicals
petrochemicals.description: Hydrocarbon fuels and feedstocks for plastics, resins, and backup generator fuel.
petrochemicals.long_description:
The crude oil and natural gas products that supply both fuel and chemical feedstocks. Natural gas is the fuel for the onsite gas turbines increasingly being built for direct datacenter power supply. Diesel fuels the backup generators that every datacenter still keeps onsite for emergencies. Crude oil refines into a range of intermediate chemicals — ethylene becomes plastic cable insulation, BPA and epichlorohydrin become the epoxy resins used in circuit boards and chip packaging. Even datacenters being built around renewable and nuclear power still depend on these hydrocarbons for backup and for the plastics inside their equipment.

Natural gas is the most directly relevant because it's the fuel underneath the fastest-growing piece of datacenter generation. Pipeline capacity to specific datacenter sites can become a real constraint independent of overall gas availability.

construction_materials.name: Construction Materials
construction_materials.description: Iron, steel, cement, and aggregates for the building shell and foundations.
construction_materials.long_description:
The bulk inputs that go into the building itself. Iron ore and scrap steel feed the steel mills that produce the structural beams and rebar. Coking coal is needed to actually smelt iron into steel. Cement and aggregates (sand, gravel, crushed stone) combine into the concrete that gets poured for foundations and slabs. These are the largest tonnage inputs in the entire chain — a single hyperscale campus uses millions of cubic feet of concrete and tens of thousands of tonnes of steel.

The most interesting dynamics here aren't supply chokepoints but regional capacity — most of these materials are too heavy to ship long distances economically, so where you can build a datacenter is partly determined by which steel mills and cement plants are within trucking range and aren't already booked up.

quartz_silica.name: Quartz & Silica
quartz_silica.description: Mined quartzite refined into silicon and fiber-optic glass.
quartz_silica.long_description:
Mined quartz rock, refined into different grades for very different uses. Metallurgical-grade quartz is the bulk material that gets reduced into silicon metal — the starting point for both solar panels and computer chips. High-purity quartz is a much rarer grade used to make the crucibles that grow silicon ingots and the glass inside fiber optic cables. The high-purity grade comes almost entirely from a single deposit in Spruce Pine, North Carolina — a quiet near-monopoly that the entire global semiconductor industry depends on.

The Spruce Pine concentration is the watched item — any disruption there ripples through both chip and fiber optic supply chains.

other_specialty.name: Other Specialty Inputs
other_specialty.description: Water, boron, and other narrow-use raw inputs scattered through the chain.
other_specialty.long_description:
A handful of materials scattered through the chain that don't fit cleanly into other categories. Water is the cooling input that's increasingly becoming a real siting constraint for datacenters — campuses consume millions of gallons annually. Boron makes specialty glass and goes into the NdFeB magnets that drive motors and disk drives. Arsenic and phosphorus are the chemical partners that pair with gallium and indium to make the wafers underlying laser and power chips. Soda ash is a flux used in making solar glass.

Water is the most strategically important — water rights are now part of the negotiation for every new hyperscale campus and a major reason some regions can't host them at all.

processors.name: Processors
processors.description: The chips that actually run AI workloads, plus the supporting silicon feeding them.
processors.long_description:
The chips that do the actual AI work. GPUs do the heavy lifting — they crunch the math that trains and runs AI models. CPUs sit next to them handling everything else, like keeping the operating system running and moving data around. NICs and DPUs are smaller chips that take care of networking so the CPUs don't get bogged down. All three are made in the same handful of advanced chip factories.

GPUs are the most supply-constrained part of the entire AI build — every hyperscaler is competing for the same Nvidia, AMD, and TSMC manufacturing capacity.

compute_memory.name: Compute-Side Memory
compute_memory.description: High-bandwidth memory bonded to AI chips so they don't sit idle.
compute_memory.long_description:
The high-bandwidth memory bonded right next to the GPU. AI workloads move enormous amounts of data in and out of the chip thousands of times per second, and regular memory can't keep up — so a special kind of memory called HBM is stacked directly alongside the GPU, with thousands of tiny vertical wires connecting them. This setup feeds the GPU at terabytes per second. Without enough HBM bandwidth, the GPU sits idle waiting for data.

HBM is supplied by just three companies — SK Hynix, Samsung, and Micron — and demand consistently outruns supply.

board_integration.name: Board & Integration
board_integration.description: The multi-layer PCBs that physically host the chip assemblies.
board_integration.long_description:
The motherboards that physically hold the chips together. A server board is a multi-layer circuit board with copper wiring etched into it, connecting the processors, memory, power supplies, and networking onto a single platform that slides into a rack. AI server boards are unusually complex — modern designs have 20+ layers and have to carry signals at very high speeds without interference.

Most of these are built by a small group of Taiwanese ODMs — Foxconn, Quanta, Wiwynn — that manufacture for both branded vendors and direct-to-hyperscaler.

chip_power_delivery.name: Chip Power Delivery
chip_power_delivery.description: Steps rack power down to the low voltage chips actually run on.
chip_power_delivery.long_description:
The small power supplies sitting next to every chip. The power coming into a server rack is at hundreds of volts — but the chips themselves run at less than 1 volt. Something has to step it down in stages, and that's what PSUs and VRMs do. Modern AI accelerators draw enormous amounts of power, so getting the right voltage to the chip reliably is harder than it sounds.

The most efficient versions of these increasingly use gallium nitride (GaN) chips inside them, which links this subgroup back to gallium supply at the raw material layer.

chip_thermal.name: Chip Thermal
chip_thermal.description: Direct-to-chip cooling hardware pulling heat off GPUs into the liquid loop.
chip_thermal.long_description:
The metal plates that pull heat directly off the chips. Modern AI chips run so hot that air cooling can't keep up — you have to mount a metal plate directly onto the chip and pump liquid coolant through tiny channels carved into it. That liquid carries the heat away to the rest of the cooling system. Every GPU and CPU in a modern AI rack has one of these on top of it.

Boyd, AVC, and CoolIT are the main suppliers, and demand has scaled dramatically with the shift from air to liquid cooling.

working_memory.name: Working Memory
working_memory.description: DRAM modules feeding the CPU; the system's main memory pool.
working_memory.long_description:
The main memory feeding the CPU — like RAM in a regular computer, just much bigger. Unlike HBM (which sits next to the GPU), this memory plugs into the motherboard in stick form and serves the CPU's general-purpose work: managing the operating system, holding data the GPU isn't actively crunching, coordinating workloads. Modern AI servers can hold terabytes of this memory per node.

Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron supply almost all of it, the same three companies that make HBM.

hot_storage.name: Hot Storage
hot_storage.description: NVMe SSDs and their flash for low-latency access to active data.
hot_storage.long_description:
The fast SSDs that hold data the system is actively using. When an AI model needs to load training data or save its state, it reads from hot storage. These are flash-based drives that can read and write data thousands of times faster than traditional hard drives. Modern enterprise SSDs hit hundreds of terabytes per drive and are packaged in slim form factors that slide into a server.

The flash chips inside them come from Samsung, SK Hynix, Kioxia, and Micron — the same companies that dominate memory more broadly.

cold_storage.name: Cold Storage
cold_storage.description: High-capacity hard drives for archival and backup tiers.
cold_storage.long_description:
The traditional hard drives that hold data the system rarely touches. Spinning-disk drives are far slower than SSDs but also far cheaper per terabyte, which makes them the right choice for archival data, backups, and the long tail of files an AI training run might need access to but isn't reading constantly. Modern datacenter HDDs are sealed with helium inside so the platters can spin faster without air resistance.

Three companies make all of them — Seagate, Western Digital, and Toshiba — and they're approaching 30+ TB per drive.

switching_silicon.name: Switching Silicon
switching_silicon.description: Custom ASICs that forward packets at terabit scale.
switching_silicon.long_description:
The chips inside network switches that decide where each packet of data should go. When a GPU in one server sends data to a GPU in another server, a network switch has to route that packet to the right place at extreme speed. Switch ASICs are custom chips designed for exactly that job — modern ones move 51 to 102 terabits per second.

Broadcom dominates this market with the Tomahawk and Jericho families, with Nvidia and Cisco competing more recently.

switching_boxes.name: Switching Boxes
switching_boxes.description: The assembled switches that route traffic between racks and buildings.
switching_boxes.long_description:
The actual switch hardware that goes into a rack. A switch ASIC by itself is just a chip — to make it useful you have to package it with optics, cooling, management software, and a chassis. That's what a switching box is. These are what physically connect the racks in a datacenter to each other and to the outside world.

Arista, Cisco, and Nvidia (via Mellanox) are the main vendors. White-box switches from ODMs are increasingly common at hyperscale.

optical_io.name: Optical I/O
optical_io.description: Hardware converting electrical signals to light for high-speed fiber links.
optical_io.long_description:
The hardware that converts electrical signals into light and back. Inside a server everything moves as electricity, but for any distance more than a few meters you have to convert to light pulses traveling through fiber. Optical transceivers do that conversion — they're plug-in modules that sit at each end of a fiber connection. New designs called co-packaged optics integrate the conversion directly into the switch chip to save power, which is becoming necessary at the highest speeds.

Coherent, Lumentum, and Innolight are the main transceiver makers. Co-packaged optics is the emerging shift.

cabling.name: Cabling
cabling.description: The fiber and copper actually carrying signals between equipment.
cabling.long_description:
The fiber and copper that physically carry the signals. Fiber optic cable is the long-distance medium — strands of specially-doped glass that guide light pulses across racks, buildings, and continents. Short-distance connections inside a rack often use copper instead, in the form of direct-attach cables. A single AI cluster can need millions of meters of fiber.

Corning, Prysmian, Sumitomo Electric, and a handful of others dominate fiber. Amphenol and Molex dominate copper interconnect.

chip_level_cooling.name: Chip-Level Cooling
chip_level_cooling.description: In-rack manifolds and connectors feeding coolant to each compute tray.
chip_level_cooling.long_description:
The plumbing that delivers coolant to each individual server. After the cold plates on each chip absorb heat into liquid, that liquid has to flow back out of the rack to be cooled and recirculated. Manifolds are the in-rack tubing that distributes coolant to each server tray. Quick-disconnect fittings let servers be removed for maintenance without leaks.

Parker Hannifin, CPC, and Staubli supply most of the precision fittings, while rack makers integrate them into the rack design.

rack_level_cooling.name: Rack-Level Cooling
rack_level_cooling.description: Pump units circulating coolant between rack manifolds and facility loops.
rack_level_cooling.long_description:
The pump units that circulate coolant between racks and the rest of the cooling system. A coolant distribution unit (CDU) is essentially a sophisticated pump and heat exchanger. It pulls warm coolant out of the racks, transfers the heat into the facility's main cooling loop, and pushes cool coolant back into the racks. They range from rack-sized units serving a single rack up to room-sized units serving entire rows.

Vertiv, Boyd, and CoolIT are the main suppliers, and demand has scaled rapidly with the shift to liquid cooling.

heat_rejection.name: Heat Rejection
heat_rejection.description: Chillers and towers expelling facility heat to the atmosphere.
heat_rejection.long_description:
The equipment that ultimately dumps the heat outside. Once the cooling system has collected heat from the racks, it has to get rid of it. Chillers compress refrigerant to move heat from one place to another. Cooling towers spray water that evaporates and carries heat into the air. Heat exchangers transfer heat between different fluid loops. Every datacenter uses some combination of these depending on its climate.

Trane, Carrier, and Johnson Controls dominate chillers. SPX, Baltimore Aircoil, and Evapco dominate cooling towers.

air_handling.name: Air Handling
air_handling.description: Air-based cooling for networking, storage, and equipment that doesn't need liquid.
air_handling.long_description:
The air-based cooling for the parts of the facility that don't get the liquid treatment. Networking equipment, storage drives, and various ancillary gear still rely on air cooling, even in an otherwise liquid-cooled facility. CRAH units (computer room air handlers) and fan walls push cooled air through these zones.

Vertiv, Stulz, and Trane supply most of these. The market is mature and the technology is well understood.

switching_protection.name: Switching & Protection
switching_protection.description: Gear routing and isolating power flows inside the facility.
switching_protection.long_description:
The gear that routes power flows inside the facility and protects against faults. Medium-voltage switchgear is the electrical equivalent of a circuit breaker panel, but for the much higher voltages running between the datacenter's main feed and its various subsystems. Automatic transfer switches sense when the utility power fails and seamlessly switch the facility over to backup generators.

ABB, Schneider Electric, and Eaton dominate this market. Lead times have stretched significantly as datacenter demand has surged.

voltage_conversion.name: Voltage Conversion
voltage_conversion.description: Transformers stepping medium-voltage feeds down to facility utilization voltage.
voltage_conversion.long_description:
The transformers that step medium-voltage power down to something the equipment can use. Power arrives at a datacenter at high voltages (saves losses over distance) but the IT equipment runs at much lower voltages. Step-down transformers do that conversion. A hyperscale campus might use dozens of these distributed throughout the facility.

ABB, Hitachi Energy, and Eaton are the main suppliers, and transformer lead times are now a major constraint on datacenter delivery timelines — sometimes 144+ weeks.

backup_energy.name: Backup Energy
backup_energy.description: UPS and battery systems holding the load through utility disturbances.
backup_energy.long_description:
The UPS systems and batteries that hold the load when utility power fails. A UPS (uninterruptible power supply) bridges the few seconds between when the grid fails and when the backup generators kick in. Behind every UPS is a stack of batteries — historically lead-acid, increasingly lithium iron phosphate. BESS (battery energy storage systems) are larger battery installations that can also play a role in grid services, not just backup.

Vertiv, Schneider Electric, and Eaton dominate UPS. Tesla, Fluence, and CATL dominate grid-scale BESS.

distribution_paths.name: Distribution Paths
distribution_paths.description: Busways, PDUs, and cables delivering power along rack rows.
distribution_paths.long_description:
The actual physical paths power takes through the facility. After voltage conversion, power has to be delivered to each rack — busways run overhead carrying power along rows of racks, PDUs distribute it to individual racks, and various cables route it through the rest of the facility. These are the unglamorous but essential plumbing of a datacenter's electrical system.

Schneider Electric, Eaton, and Vertiv dominate the busway and PDU markets. Cabling is supplied by Prysmian, Nexans, and Southwire.

last_mile_backup.name: Last-Mile Backup
last_mile_backup.description: Diesel and gas generators providing extended-runtime backup behind the UPS.
last_mile_backup.long_description:
The diesel and gas generators that provide extended-runtime backup. UPS systems can only hold the load for minutes — for anything longer, datacenters rely on combustion-engine generators. These are typically sized to run the entire facility for days on stored fuel. Every datacenter still has them, even those built around renewable or nuclear primary power.

Caterpillar, Cummins, and Kohler are the dominant vendors. Diesel is still the most common fuel but natural gas is growing as a cleaner alternative.

gas_fired.name: Gas-Fired Generation
gas_fired.description: Onsite natural gas plants bypassing grid bottlenecks for new capacity.
gas_fired.long_description:
The fastest way to get a dedicated gigawatt of power to a datacenter today. With grid connection waits now stretching past five years in most US markets, hyperscalers are increasingly building their own gas power plants on the campus, behind the meter. The group spans three different turbine types — large frame turbines, smaller jet-engine-derived aeroderivatives, and modular reciprocating engines — plus the equipment that handles heat recovery and emissions.

Aeroderivative turbines are currently the workaround everyone is using because they ship faster than the larger frame turbines, which have delivery times stretching into 2029.

nuclear.name: Nuclear Generation
nuclear.description: Reactors providing 24/7 carbon-free baseload via PPAs or future onsite SMRs.
nuclear.long_description:
Reactors providing round-the-clock carbon-free power. The current wave includes recommissioning existing reactors that were retired (Three Mile Island is restarting for Microsoft) and a new generation of smaller, factory-built reactors called SMRs that several companies are building specifically for datacenter customers. Nuclear is the most-watched future addition to the datacenter generation mix because it's the only practical source of 24/7 carbon-free power at scale.

Constellation, Vistra, and Duke supply the conventional side. Oklo, X-energy, and Kairos Power are the leading SMR developers.

renewable.name: Renewable Generation
renewable.description: Solar, wind, and inverters delivering variable clean power to the campus.
renewable.long_description:
Solar panels, wind turbines, and the inverters that convert their output to grid-compatible electricity. Datacenters are major buyers of renewable power, but their 24/7 load doesn't match the variable output of solar and wind — so renewable generation typically gets paired with batteries or other firm power sources. Most hyperscalers have multi-gigawatt renewable power purchase agreements running alongside their other generation sources.

First Solar (CdTe panels), Trina, and Longi dominate solar manufacturing. Vestas, GE Vernova, and Siemens Gamesa dominate wind.

long_duration_storage.name: Long-Duration Storage
long_duration_storage.description: Flow batteries and emerging multi-hour storage pairing with renewables.
long_duration_storage.long_description:
Batteries designed to discharge over hours, not minutes. Pairing renewables with storage usually means lithium-ion batteries, but they only hold a few hours of charge before degrading. Vanadium redox flow batteries are an emerging alternative where the energy is stored in liquid tanks of vanadium electrolyte — they can discharge for 8+ hours, last 25+ years without degrading, and scale by adding more tanks. The whole subgroup is small today but growing as longer-duration storage becomes critical for renewable-heavy campuses.

Invinity Energy, Sumitomo Electric, and VRB Energy are the main flow battery vendors.

distributed_generation.name: Distributed Generation
distributed_generation.description: Fuel cells and modular onsite generators for distributed power.
distributed_generation.long_description:
Modular onsite generators that don't fit the centralized power plant pattern. Fuel cells are the main example — they generate electricity through a chemical reaction rather than combustion, which makes them quieter, lower-emission, and easier to deploy in distributed locations across a campus. Stargate Abilene reportedly includes Bloom Energy fuel cells as part of its generation mix.

Bloom Energy, FuelCell Energy, and Plug Power are the main suppliers.

grid_interface.name: Grid Interface
grid_interface.description: Step-up transformers and substation gear connecting plants to the wider grid.
grid_interface.long_description:
The transformers and high-voltage gear connecting the power plant to the wider electric grid. Even datacenters with onsite power generation typically stay connected to the grid as a backup and as a way to sell excess power. Generator step-up transformers convert plant output to transmission voltage. HV switchgear protects the connection. HV transmission cable physically carries the power.

Hitachi Energy, GE Vernova, and Hyundai Electric dominate large transformers. Lead times here are some of the worst in the entire chain.

structural_shell.name: Structural Shell
structural_shell.description: The steel, concrete, and rebar carrying the building's load.
structural_shell.long_description:
The actual building. Datacenters are surprisingly heavy because the racks inside them are dense and concentrated — a single AI rack can weigh as much as a car sitting on a small footprint. That means the foundations have to be much thicker than a normal commercial building, and the steel frame has to carry serious load even when the building is only one story. A hyperscale campus uses 20,000+ tonnes of steel and millions of cubic feet of concrete.

The materials themselves aren't exotic — just steel, cement, and rebar — but datacenter construction is now big enough to noticeably tighten US steel mill capacity.

white_space_buildout.name: White-Space Build-Out
white_space_buildout.description: Raised flooring and interior fitout inside the IT halls.
white_space_buildout.long_description:
The interior fit-out of the IT halls. Raised access flooring is the main element — a modular floor system about 18 inches off the slab, with removable panels that let cabling, cooling pipes, and power lines run underneath. The IT racks sit on top. Some modern designs are moving away from raised floors in favor of overhead distribution, but most facilities still use them.

Tate, ASM, and Haworth are the main suppliers.

life_safety.name: Life Safety
life_safety.description: Fire suppression and security protecting the people and the equipment.
life_safety.long_description:
The systems that protect the people and the equipment. Fire suppression in a datacenter can't use water as the primary agent because it would destroy the IT equipment — instead, special clean-agent gases (FM-200, Novec 1230) flood the rooms and starve a fire of oxygen without leaving residue. Security systems handle perimeter fencing, badge access, surveillance, and intrusion detection across what are increasingly hardened campuses.

Johnson Controls, Honeywell, and 3M supply fire suppression. Various integrators handle security.

site.name: Site
site.description: The land, water, and grid interconnect rights underpinning the campus.
site.long_description:
The land, water rights, and grid interconnect rights underneath the campus. A hyperscale datacenter needs 1,000+ acres of land, significant water access for cooling, and a pre-negotiated grid connection. All three are getting harder to secure. Land near major transmission lines is scarce, water rights are politically contested in dry regions, and grid interconnect queues stretch years. These rights are increasingly the actual bottleneck on where new campuses can be built.

Crusoe, Tract, and Stack Infrastructure are among the firms acquiring and developing sites at scale.

patterned_wafers.name: Patterned Wafers
patterned_wafers.description: Silicon wafers that have been through the fab carrying actual chip designs.
patterned_wafers.long_description:
Silicon wafers that have already been through the chip factory and now carry actual chip designs etched into them. A wafer starts as a blank polished silicon disc — by the time it leaves the fab it's been through hundreds of process steps that have layered, patterned, and etched circuit designs into it. Each wafer contains dozens or hundreds of individual chip dies that get separated and packaged downstream.

The most advanced wafers (5nm, 3nm, 2nm) are made only by TSMC and Samsung. The mature-node wafers (28nm and older) are made by a wider group including GlobalFoundries and UMC.

silicon_feedstock.name: Silicon Feedstock
silicon_feedstock.description: The progressively purified silicon between quartzite and finished wafers.
silicon_feedstock.long_description:
The progressively purified silicon between raw quartz rock and finished wafers. It takes multiple chemical and physical steps to turn quartzite into the perfect single crystals needed for chips. First, quartz is reduced into silicon metal (98% pure). Then it gets refined into polysilicon (99.9999% pure). Then it gets grown into giant single crystal ingots and sliced into wafers. Each step has its own specialized producers and supply chain.

The most concentrated point is high-purity quartz, where nearly all the world's supply comes from a single deposit in Spruce Pine, North Carolina.

advanced_packaging.name: Advanced Packaging
advanced_packaging.description: Bonding chips, memory, and substrates into finished GPU and CPU modules.
advanced_packaging.long_description:
The step that turns bare chips into finished products. When a chip comes out of the factory, it's just a tiny square of silicon — you can't actually plug it into anything. Advanced packaging is the assembly process that bonds the chip to memory, wires it up for high-speed communication, and mounts it on a substrate you can connect to a circuit board. Modern AI chips have this assembly step done by TSMC using a process called CoWoS, which stacks memory right next to the chip so data can move between them at extreme speeds.

CoWoS capacity is the real bottleneck behind Nvidia GPU supply — TSMC can make the chips faster than it can package them. The substrate material that goes underneath is made almost entirely by one Japanese company, Ajinomoto.

fab_chemistry.name: Fab Chemistry
fab_chemistry.description: Photoresists, slurries, gases, and ultra-pure water consumed in chip manufacturing.
fab_chemistry.long_description:
The specialty chemicals and gases consumed inside chip factories. Making a chip involves hundreds of process steps, and many of them require very specific chemistries. Photoresist is the light-sensitive coating that lets patterns be projected onto the wafer. CMP slurries polish each layer flat between steps. Specialty solvents and ultra-pure water clean the wafer between every step. These chemistries are consumed in enormous volumes per fab — a leading-edge fab uses millions of gallons of ultra-pure water per day.

Photoresist for the most advanced chips is dominated by JSR, Tokyo Ohka Kogyo, and Shin-Etsu — all Japanese — making it a strategic concentration point.

compound_semi_wafers.name: Compound Semiconductor Wafers
compound_semi_wafers.description: Non-silicon wafers like InP and GaN for lasers and power switches.
compound_semi_wafers.long_description:
Wafers made from silicon-substitute materials for specific high-performance jobs. Silicon is the workhorse semiconductor but it has limits — for lasers, very-high-frequency electronics, and high-efficiency power switches, materials like indium phosphide (InP), gallium arsenide (GaAs), and gallium nitride (GaN) work much better. These compound semiconductor wafers are far smaller volumes than silicon wafers but are essential for the specific applications they serve.

InP wafers are particularly relevant to AI infrastructure because they underlie the lasers in every high-speed optical transceiver, and InP wafer capacity is a tracked supply constraint.

specialty_alloys.name: Specialty Alloys & Ceramics
specialty_alloys.description: Superalloys, electrical steel, magnets, and ceramics for turbines and transformers.
specialty_alloys.long_description:
Engineered metal alloys and ceramic materials with very specific high-performance properties. Nickel single-crystal superalloys can withstand the extreme temperatures inside a gas turbine blade. Grain-oriented electrical steel (GOES) has magnetic properties that make it ideal for transformer cores. Stainless steel resists corrosion in cooling loops. NdFeB magnets are the strongest commercially available. None of these are made by simply melting one element — they're carefully formulated mixtures of multiple elements processed in specific ways.

GOES electrical steel is one of the most consequential bottlenecks behind the transformer shortage that's now constraining datacenter buildout timelines.

battery_intermediates.name: Battery Cells & Precursors
battery_intermediates.description: Finished lithium cells plus the cathode, anode, and electrolyte chemistries inside.
battery_intermediates.long_description:
The lithium batteries that hold electricity for backup and storage, plus the materials that go inside them. A battery cell has three parts that matter — a cathode that stores energy, an anode that releases it, and a liquid electrolyte between them that carries the charge back and forth. Datacenter UPS systems and grid storage almost all use LFP cells (lithium iron phosphate), because that chemistry is cheaper and safer than the kind used in EVs. Vanadium flow batteries are an emerging alternative for storing power over longer durations.

Almost every step of LFP cell production is concentrated in China — about 95% of the cathode material is processed there.

nuclear_fuel.name: Nuclear Fuel Forms
nuclear_fuel.description: Enriched uranium fuel assemblies and the zirconium tubing surrounding them.
nuclear_fuel.long_description:
The processed fuel assemblies that go inside reactors. Uranium has to go through several steps before it can power a reactor — mining produces raw uranium ore, which gets converted into uranium hexafluoride gas, which gets enriched (concentrating the fissile isotope), which gets pressed into fuel pellets, which get stacked inside zirconium tubes (cladding), which get bundled into fuel assemblies. The new SMR reactors require a more enriched version called HALEU that almost nobody currently produces.

HALEU is the most acute bottleneck — only Russia and China produce it at commercial scale today, and Western SMR projects need it to actually fuel up.

solar_intermediates.name: Solar Intermediates
solar_intermediates.description: Thin films, conductive pastes, and tempered glass feeding solar panel assembly.
solar_intermediates.long_description:
The processed materials that go into a solar panel between the raw silicon or thin-film and the finished panel. Silver paste forms the front-side conductors that collect electricity from each cell. CdTe film is the active layer in First Solar's thin-film panels (a separate technology from silicon). Solar glass is the tempered, low-iron glass on the front of every panel.

Silver paste is the most demand-sensitive — solar manufacturing consumes 10–15% of global mined silver and that share grows every year.

specialty_fluids_gases.name: Specialty Fluids & Gases
specialty_fluids_gases.description: Coolants, refrigerants, transformer oils, and insulating gases throughout the facility.
specialty_fluids_gases.long_description:
The processed liquids and gases used throughout datacenter equipment. Engineered coolants flow through liquid cooling loops. Refrigerants run inside chillers. Transformer oil insulates and cools transformer cores. XLPE is the plastic insulation around HV cables. SF6 (and its replacements) is the insulating gas inside high-voltage switchgear. None of these are exotic in small quantities, but datacenters use them at massive scale.

The most strategically watched is SF6 — it's a potent greenhouse gas and is being phased out in favor of newer alternatives, which is reshaping the global switchgear market.

polymers.name: Polymers & Composites
polymers.description: Epoxy resins and fiberglass forming substrates, laminates, and turbine blades.
polymers.long_description:
Engineered plastics and reinforcement materials used throughout the build. Epoxy resin is the matrix that holds together both ABF substrates (under every chip) and FR-4 circuit boards (under every other chip). Fiberglass reinforces those boards, as well as wind turbine blades and cooling tower fill. These materials don't get headlines but they're embedded in essentially every electrical and structural product in the chain.

Hexion, Olin, and Kukdo dominate epoxy. Owens Corning, Jushi, and Saint-Gobain dominate fiberglass.

discrete_passives.name: Discrete Passives
discrete_passives.description: Capacitors and other small board components shared across nearly every device.
discrete_passives.long_description:
The small electronic components soldered onto every board — capacitors, resistors, inductors. They don't process information themselves, they just shape the electrical environment that other components need to work in. The most strategically important type for AI infrastructure is tantalum capacitors, which provide highly reliable energy storage at small sizes — every server board has many of them, even though each one is tiny.

Tantalum capacitor production is concentrated in a handful of manufacturers (Kemet/Yageo, AVX, Vishay) and tantalum supply itself is a watched item.
